Our responses and the original authors' own show one dominant vehicle plus a heavy tail of distinct minority vehicles. "Time" is one of our least diverse topics, so the example is a favorable case, not a representative one. Second, the paper measures homogeneity against an undemanding null: responses to unrelated prompts. Under a more demanding null (same-prompt responses expressing genuinely different ideas), 20%-32% of such pairs already exceed the paper's 0.8 convergence threshold. A residual effect survives this null. The paper's same-prompt pairs exceed 0.8 roughly two to three times as often as our different-idea pairs. Much of what the paper calls homogeneity is the shared geometry of answering the same prompt. The remaining measurements lack any null: no human baseline is collected, and the model-indistinguishability statistic has no null. Third, the paper concludes that inference-time interventions are inadequate for combating the Artificial Hivemind, writing that "more generalizable solutions are needed at the model training level." We show that this conclusion is unsupported in three ways, and that an inference-time intervention (prompting) reliably raises measured response diversity. We do not resolve whether the Artificial Hivemind is real. We show that the published evidence does not establish it.

unique.title: Measuring Collapse and Correction in Homogeneous-Panel LLM Debate
unique.abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) debate is often evaluated by whether final answers improve, but a changed answer is not necessarily a better one: the same discussion can correct an initially wrong majority or collapse an initially correct one. Standard final-accuracy evaluations conflate these opposing transitions. We introduce an auditable protocol for homogeneous debate on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) that records each run as a transition ledger over collapse, correction, onset, and signed intervention utility. On 6,925 MMLU-Pro debates, the protocol records 253 collapses together with the corrections that offset them, and the correction side changes how interventions should be judged. Replay experiments reveal the central tradeoff: freezing every debate prevents 251 collapses but loses 804 corrections under equal weights, and a leave-one-model-out probe-gated freeze that is tuned for net utility never fires, so collapse prevention alone can recommend the wrong policy. A compact pre-debate 8-probe screen is a triage signal: its unadjusted family-level association with conditional-collapse risk is high (G=7, Spearman $ρ$ = 0.893, exact two-sided p = 0.0123), but initial-majority accuracy is a close comparator ($ρ$ = -0.821; family partial $ρ$ = 0.767, p = 0.0877), so we do not treat it as calibrated or capability-adjusted prediction. Round-level traces localize many collapses to the first debate round, where early disagreement can precede both collapses and corrections. Reasoning-mode models, including one model at two reasoning-effort levels, also show both collapses and corrections. We release replayable schemas, coders, audits, cost cards, and zero-API rebuild scripts so future model rows can be compared under the same denominators and signed utility ledger.

unique.title: ResComEmb: Effective and Efficient Multimodal Embedding via Residual Homogeneity Compression
unique.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown strong potential for universal multimodal representation learning. However, existing methods either compress each input into a single vector, limiting fine-grained expressiveness, or retain long sequences of visual-token vectors, incurring substantial storage and interaction costs. To resolve this trade-off, we propose ResComEmb, a trainable framework for effective and efficient universal multi-vector multimodal embedding. ResComEmb first encodes each input at native dynamic resolution into ordered global, intermediate, and fine-grained views. After MLLM contextualization and embedding projection, a trainable Residual Homogeneity Compression (RHC) module reduces within-granularity redundancy and cross-granularity repetition under explicit visual token budgets. Then, ResComEmb introduces a length-adaptive Bidirectional Late-Interaction Matching mechanism for robust query-document scoring, which averages the strongest token-level matches in each direction and combines the two scores using a weight based on how many valid tokens each side has. Extensive experiments on MMEB, ViDoRe V1, and ViDoRe V2 show that ResComEmb produces higher-quality universal multimodal embeddings than VLM2Vec-V2, and outperforms ColQwen2.5 in visual document retrieval using only 37.5% of its full visual token budget, demonstrating a favorable effectiveness-efficiency trade-off.

unique.title: Gap Detection: Mitigating Homogenization through Demand and Defensibility
unique.abstract: Language models often produce semantically similar answers to open-ended questions, even when many plausible alternatives exist. Generating useful alternatives requires identifying both what the query calls for and what existing responses already cover. We introduce Gap Detection, a framework that searches for relevant but unoccupied directions in a shared text embedding space. Its objective, GapScore, combines query relevance (Demand) with dissimilarity to the nearest existing item (Defensibility). The framework optimizes this product on the unit sphere, maps candidate directions to concept words with a language model, and uses task-specific filtering and constrained prompting to turn those concepts into text. On five curated topics and 90 INFINITY-CHAT queries, the reported mean relative reductions in output Collision are 12.8% and 10.8%, respectively. We also instantiate the framework for generative engine optimization over four product markets and for iterative synthetic-data augmentation. In the latter setting, with 100 training examples per method, Gap Detection reduces Collision from 0.324 to 0.298 relative to undirected accumulation and increases the Vendi Score from 27.16 to 29.20; the accuracy difference is one example on a 40-example test set. Component ablations expose the trade-off between semantic separation and relevance, while also showing that better direction scores do not uniformly yield better downstream metrics. These results support explicit gap search as a practical mechanism for diversifying content, with task validity checked separately from geometric novelty.

unique.title: Exact Makespan Bounds and the GPipe Homogeneity Bias for Heterogeneous LLM Inference Pipelines
unique.abstract: We give an exact critical-path characterization of the makespan of micro-batch pipelines serving LLMs on heterogeneous GPU clusters, quantifying how the classic homogeneous GPipe formula errs. In the pure-forward, communication-free, infinite-buffer setting, T(M) = (M-1)tau_max + Sum_j tau_j, where tau_j is stage j's per-micro-batch service time and M the micro-batch count (Theorem 1). Under asynchronous communication -- modern NCCL-based serving -- it extends to T(M) = Sum_j tau_j + Sum_j d_j + (M-1)tau_max, with Sum_j d_j a purely additive constant (Theorem 2); under blocking communication, T(M) = (M-1)sigma_max + Sum_s sigma_s with sigma_s = tau_s + d_s, so communication enters the steady-state slope iff some d_s > tau_max - tau_s (Theorem 3). These results quantify the GPipe overestimate, decompose the bias into a homogeneity term Sum_j (tau_max - tau_j) and a communication-ignoring term Sum_j d_j, and imply that balancing per-stage compute dominates communication reduction for steady-state throughput. A real system with partial overlap is sandwiched between Theorems 2 and 3, with a closed-form bound on the overlap throughput gain. All claims are validated pointwise (error < 10^-9) on eleven configurations and a 1.6x10^5-point fuzz, including a mixed RTX 5090/3090/GTX 1070 partition. We situate the results in flow-shop scheduling and list open extensions: bandwidth-limited communication, bounded buffers, prefill-decode interleaving.

unique.title: Does AI-Assisted Development Homogenize Software? An Empirical Study of Code Similarity, Quality, and Evolution
unique.abstract: AI-assisted software development is evolving from interactive LLM assistance toward agentic systems that autonomously perform software engineering tasks, yet the effects of this shift remain insufficiently understood. We present an empirical study of 50 long-lived Java and Python open-source projects across three eras: pre-LLM, potentially LLM-assisted, and detected agentic development. Using snapshots from Software Heritage, we examine code similarity, software quality, and software evolution. Similarity is measured semantically through embedding-based cosine similarity and syntactically through CodeBLEU*. Quality is assessed with SonarQube metrics covering maintainability, complexity, reliability, and security. Evolution is characterized by annualized growth rates of LOC, functions, classes, files, and statements, and by commit activity in the three months preceding each snapshot. Results show no consistent evidence of increased similarity as semantic and syntactic similarity decreased significantly in Java for both the LLM and agentic eras relative to the pre-LLM era, while Python showed no significant differences. Software quality remained largely stable, although the agentic era showed significantly lower code-smell and SQALE index densities. Structural growth was generally lower in the agentic era, particularly for files, whereas development activity increased moderately in Java, especially in commits and added lines. These findings challenge the assumption that LLM- and agent-assisted development necessarily homogenizes code, degrades quality, or accelerates growth.

unique.title: Evaluating Cultural Knowledge Editing in Vision-Language Models
unique.abstract: Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs) frequently fail to recognize culture-specific concepts, especially from underrepresented regions. Effectively injecting this long-tail knowledge into existing models remains a challenge. In this work, we investigate knowledge editing as a targeted alternative by introducing CulturalBind, a benchmark comprising 3.2K images of 1K concepts from 6 domains, designed to evaluate culture-aware cross-modal knowledge as well as concept-level knowledge editing in VLMs. Pre-edit evaluation reveals that textual and visual knowledge is decoupled: models often demonstrate text-based knowledge of cultural concepts but fail to identify them from images. We then evaluate editing methods in single and sequential scenarios. Although current methods successfully correct individual visual recognition errors, they exhibit low cross-modal portability, failing to integrate edits into the model's broader parametric knowledge. Furthermore, performance degrades rapidly under sequential editing, highlighting the need for comprehensive adaptation approaches that better consolidate multimodal knowledge over time.

unique.title: Revisiting LLM Homogeneity Through a Multidimensional Lens
unique.abstract: Concerns about LLM homogeneity are typically quantified with embedding similarity, which reduces two texts to a single score. We revisit homogeneity with 25 interpretable metrics spanning five dimensions: semantic, lexical, syntactic, structural, and stylistic & presentational. A human study shows that perceived similarity depends on both content (what responses say) and form (how they say it), yet embedding similarity correlates less with human meaning judgments than sentence-level matching ($ρ=0.417$ vs. $0.606$) and not significantly with form judgments ($ρ=0.140$). Across 18 contemporary LLMs, models say similar things in different words: they share global semantics and broad linguistic profiles but remain distinct in lexical characteristics, structural patterns, and interactional conventions. Across releases from 2024 to 2026, models become more like themselves but not more like one another: among significantly changing metrics, intra-model distances decrease for 17 of 22, and inter-model distances increase for 14 of 21. Across two post-training pipelines, model-specific conventions emerge during SFT and are selectively reshaped by preference optimization. These results suggest that homogeneity is multidimensional and evolving, and that embedding similarity alone can overstate cross-model homogeneity while concealing diverging intra- and inter-model trends.

unique.title: Building and Auditing Chemical Datasets with LLMs: A General LLM-as-a-Judge Framework Applied to Homogeneous Catalytic PET Depolymerisation
unique.abstract: Large language models can rapidly extract structured multivariate experimental data from the chemistry literature, yet verifying thousands of generated records without ground truth remains difficult. We present a general, citation-grounded extraction and verification methodology centered on an independent "LLM-as-a-judge", applied to the literature on homogeneous catalytic poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) depolymerisation. In this pipeline, an extractor LLM generates schema-enforced records from research papers with citations to document chunks tagged with universally unique identifiers (UUIDs); an independent LLM judge then reads the full paper alongside each record, flags unsupported fields, and proposes cited corrections. Prompt ablations show that requiring chunk-level citations not only provides provenance down to specific paragraphs and tables but also improves extraction accuracy. Before deploying the judge at scale, we benchmarked it against manual evaluation on extractions from a hand-curated reference set of 295 ionic-liquid-catalysed PET glycolysis experiments. The judge agreed with human evaluation on 85.7% of reviewed records and was significantly more effective than a heuristic string-matching baseline at catching errors across related experiments. Deployed across 3,942 extracted records from 561 papers, the framework accepted 67.5% of them as written. Its proposed corrections concentrated on quantitative fields, where the extractor often conflated related experiments. We release the extracted dataset with the complete LLM judge audit logs, as well as the Chemistry Data Extractor Toolkit, an open-source application implementing this end-to-end pipeline in a code-free, browser-based environment for document parsing, customizable schema and prompt design, model-agnostic extraction and auditing, interactive provenance-highlighted review, and reproducible dataset bundling.

unique.title: LLMs and the Homogenization of Teaching
unique.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are known to lack diversity in open-ended text generation, a limitation that is especially consequential in education, where homogeneity can narrow the kinds of thinking and disciplinary work students are invited to do. We study diversity in two educational generation tasks: math items and essay feedback. We compare frontier and open-weight models with human-authored reference distributions using lexical, semantic, and domain-grounded measures. For math, we examine the mathematical activities students are asked to perform; for feedback, we examine the revision work requested and the rhetorical strategies used to communicate it. We evaluate direct prompting, two diversity prompting methods, and post-training. Across both tasks, directly prompted model outputs are markedly less diverse than human-authored content--78% higher on lexical (Self-BLEU) and 51% higher on semantic (embedding) similarity--and represent a narrower range of instructional forms. Diversity prompting and post-training increase variation largely through surface features without broadening the instructional repertoire. Models inherit and amplify the most normative routines of human instruction. Overcoming mode collapse in education will require richer instructional data and investment in teachers' creative capacity and professional judgment.

unique.title: Embedding Cosine Measures Text Length Before It Measures Homogenization
unique.abstract: Mean pairwise cosine similarity between transformer embeddings is a standard measure of whether online discourse is converging under generative AI. When the embeddings are mean-pooled outputs of an encoder never trained for sentence similarity, this measure mostly tracks text length. In 6.06 million Reddit comments, an uncentered DeBERTa-v3 measure had suggested that only conservative discourse broke toward homogeneity after late 2022. Truncating the same comments from 10 to 150 words raises their mean cosine by eight times the reported break. A placebo that swaps every comment for a random one of equal length reproduces 81% of the asymmetry, and a fixed-content simulation reproduces 78%. The leading principal direction carries 99.9% of raw DeBERTa homogeneity, and once length is handled the asymmetry disappears under every encoder. On 575,000 Stack Exchange answers the measure reports a post-ChatGPT homogenization of technical sites that the placebo fully reproduces, although answers grew longer. A census of 31 studies locates the risk where anisotropic encoders meet time-series or length-unequal designs. A reverse control on a well-known experiment shows that centering with renormalization can reverse a genuine effect. We propose a low-cost diagnostic protocol. Corrected measures show that the two political camps converged between 2019 and 2022 and stopped converging before ChatGPT. Cross-camp replies engage their targets more closely than same-camp replies.

unique.title: Twice-Told Critiques: Claim-Level Homogenization of Peer Review in the LLM Era
unique.abstract: Peer review relies on several readers finding different problems. We measure critique overlap in conference and journal reviews. At ICLR, measured overlap rose from 12.0% in 2026 to 21.3% in 2027, in reviews from the same stage of the review process, with year-on-year rises at NeurIPS, ICML and the F1000 and PLOS journals. A third ICLR review of a paper added 5.46 new problems to the other two in 2027, against 6.12 in 2026. We apply MELD, a detector of LLM-generated text, to all reviews. Within a paper, two reviews that MELD flags overlap more than two unflagged reviews: by 3.0 points at ICLR in 2024-2025, by 4.5 points in 2026-2027, and by 5.4 points across five journal sources. These results provide evidence that LLM-flagged reviews of one paper are less distinct from each other than unflagged reviews, and suggest that the diversity of critiques among reviews of a single paper is falling.

unique.title: Homogenizing effect of large language models (LLMs) on creative diversity: An empirical comparison of human and ChatGPT writing
unique.abstract: Generative AI systems, especially Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, have recently emerged as significant contributors to creative processes. While LLMs can produce creative content that might be as good as or even better than human-created content, their widespread use risks reducing creative diversity across groups of people. In the present research, we aimed to quantify this homogenizing effect of LLMs on creative diversity, not only at the individual level but also at the collective level. Across three preregistered studies, we analyzed 2,200 college admissions essays. Using a novel measure—the diversity growth rate—we showed that each additional human-written essay contributed more new ideas than did each additional GPT-4 essay. Notably, this difference became more pronounced as more essays were included in the analysis and persisted despite efforts to enhance AI-generated content through both prompt and parameter modifications. Overall, our findings suggest that, despite their potential to enhance individual creativity, the widespread use of LLMs could diminish the collective diversity of creative ideas. • We Introduce diversity growth rate to measure idea diversity added per creative output. • Each additional human-written essay contributes more new ideas than a GPT-generated essay. • Diversity gap widens with more essays, showing greater AI homogenization at scale. • Enhancing GPT's creative diversity through parameter- or prompt-modifications does not mitigate the diversity gap. • Our study suggests widespread LLM use could diminish collective diversity of creative ideas.
unique.journal: Computers in Human Behavior Artificial Humans

unique.title: Homogenizing Effect of a Large Language Model (LLM) on Creative Diversity: An Empirical Comparison of Human and ChatGPT Writing
unique.abstract: Generative AI systems, especially Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, have recently emerged as significant contributors to creative processes. While LLMs can produce creative content that might be as good as or even better than human creations, their widespread use risks reducing the diversity of creative outputs across groups of people. In the present research, we aimed to quantify this homogenizing effect of LLMS on collective creativity. Across three preregistered studies, we analyzed 2,200 college admissions essays. Using a novel measure—diversity growth rate—we showed that each additional human-written essay contributed more new ideas than each additional GPT-4 essay. This homogenizing effect persisted even after a range of enhancements to the diversity of the GPT-4 writings, including prompt and parameters modifications. Overall, our findings suggest that, despite improvements in individual creativity, the widespread use of LLMs could diminish the collective diversity of ideas.

unique.title: Algorithmic Assistance and the Creativity Paradox: Large Language Models, Student Writing, and Cognitive Homogenisation
unique.abstract: The adoption of large language models in higher education aids brainstorming and productivity, but raises concerns about student dependence, potentially diminishing confidence in generating original ideas independently. The paper tackles these issues by carrying out a quantitative survey on a sample size of 120 undergraduate and postgraduate students of four universities in Dublin, that is, Dublin City University, University College Dublin, Trinity College Dublin, and Technological University Dublin. The respondents were varied in their academic backgrounds; some were undergraduate or post-graduate level and this was evenly split between 46 per cent female and 54 per cent male. The survey was taking the trends of using ChatGPT, the sense of creative self-efficacy, and how dissimilar students perceived academic ideas and written work. The results suggest that there is a definite conflict in the application of AI tools. A significant number of respondents referred to ChatGPT in the context of the idea development, increased productive, and assistance at the first drafting phase. Nevertheless, a large percentage of them experienced more trouble in idea generation, and thought they were beginning to resemble the work of other students using the same system. On the whole, 67.5 per cent thought that their ideas were growing closer to those who also use ChatGPT. These results imply that the positive effects of writing with AI might be accompanied by the feeling of reduced originality. The paper highlights AI’s impact on creativity, emphasizing pedagogical strategies for fostering independent thinking and intellectual diversity in education.

unique.title: Dull Stable State: Recursive Training, Homogenization, and Security Risks in the Era of Large Language Models
unique.abstract: The rapid proliferation of large language models (LLMs) has accelerated the production of online content, yet this growth introduces a recursive dynamic: as models increasingly train on AI-generated text, the diversity and fidelity of outputs decline. Recent research identifies this phenomenon as model collapse, where recursive self-training erodes the statistical tails of language distributions, yielding homogenized and repetitive responses. Parallel studies of recommender systems highlight analogous feedback loops, including algorithmic monocultures and popularity bias, that converge toward uniformity and suppress minority content. Combined, these forces risk what may be termed a dull stable state: an equilibrium in which digital knowledge systems recycle their own outputs, losing novelty, accuracy, and epistemic richness. This state carries profound security implications. Homogenized training corpora amplify vulnerabilities to data poisoning, adversarial prompt injection, and covert manipulation, while reliance on synthetic data increases risks of privacy leakage through membership inference and undermines trust in provenance. Addressing these challenges requires robust data curation, provenance standards (e.g., watermarking, C2PA credentials), and hybrid training strategies that maintain human-authored input. The literature suggests that without such interventions, the pursuit of scale may trade diversity for stability, locking the AI ecosystem into a fragile equilibrium with degraded utility and heightened security exposure.
unique.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

unique.title: Not Homogenization but Bifurcation: Large Language Models as Cognitive Amplifiers (The AI-Induced Subjectivity Crisis Series, Paper 7)
unique.abstract: This paper constitutes Paper 7 of the AI-Induced Subjectivity Crisis Series. Contemporary discourse on the cognitive effects of large language models converges on a shared but unexamined assumption: that LLMs are a homogenizing force, producing effects of the same direction across different users, varying only in degree. This paper rejects that assumption and argues for its structural opposite. LLMs function not as tools but as cognitive amplifiers — a categorical distinction, not one of degree. Tools operate outside cognitive structure; LLMs intervene at the level at which language and thought occur, responding in real time to the user's narrative framework and returning its internal logic in a more complete, more rigorous version through the mechanism of meaning refinement. The direction of amplification is not supplied by the amplifier but by the input signal: the user's existing subjectivity structure. The paper argues for three mutually dependent propositions. First, meaning refinement and borrowed subjectivity (Liu 2026f) constitute the two dimensions of the amplifier mechanism: meaning refinement provides the force of amplification; borrowed subjectivity provides its direction. Their superposition produces not cognitive reflection but the structural reinforcement of existing cognitive tendency. Second, the same LLM mechanism produces structurally opposite effects in users with different subjectivity structures. Users with robust subjectivity structures are reinforced through two independent positive feedback loops: the reactance activation mechanism, whereby LLM's unlimited compliance triggers a demand for genuine other-friction in reality; and the confidence leverage mechanism, whereby LLM's meaning amplification is converted into the starting point for real-world action rather than consumed as a narrative endpoint. Users with fragile subjectivity structures undergo accelerated abdication of subjectivity — LLMs not only satisfy dependency needs but systematically remove the friction conditions that, in Kegan's developmental framework, are required for the transition from the Socialized Mind to the Self-Authoring Mind. Third, the antecedent variable of this mechanism — subjectivity structure strength — is logically prior to and measurably independent of LLM effects. Kegan's theory of adult development, established decades before LLMs, provides the philosophical anchor: the distinction between the Socialized Mind and the Self-Authoring Mind describes structural differences formed within genuine interpersonal friction, not reactions to any technological environment. Block and Kremen's Ego Resiliency Scale (ER89) provides an operationalization pathway, demonstrating that the differentiation axis can be independently measured prior to LLM intervention and is not a synonym for LLM effects. The historical dimension of this argument reveals a structural rupture in the history of cognitive tools. Previous cognitive inequality was located at the level of accessibility — tool democratization dissolved the inequality. LLM's cognitive inequality is located at the level of the structural effects produced during user-tool interaction: tool democratization does not dissolve this inequality but diffuses the unidirectional amplification mechanism across a larger population, simultaneously accelerating differentiation in both directions. Equality of access does not equal equality of cognitive structure. The paper further argues that LLMs introduce intra-generational differentiation at a speed unprecedented in cognitive history, and a generational fault line whose depth will only become fully visible as the first generation to form its cognitive structural foundations within a LLM-saturated environment reaches cognitive maturity. The paper passes no moral verdict on either end of the differentiation spectrum, treats the consequences of differentiation as open and condition-dependent, and explicitly stops at the philosophical argument for the mechanism. Observable indicators, institutional friction-compensation strategies, and the interaction between the differentiation axis and existing structures of social inequality are reserved as agendas for subsequent empirical and normative research.
unique.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

unique.title: Attention-Enhanced Large Language Model-Guided Semantic Fusion for Representation Learning in Historical Cultural Knowledge Graphs
unique.abstract: Historical-cultural collections contain heterogeneous descriptions that are difficult to compare as isolated records. This protocol organizes these descriptions into evidence-supported knowledge graphs and combines structural and textual representations for relation-learning tasks. The workflow comprises corpus selection and provenance recording, domain ontology design, text normalization, candidate entity detection, schema-constrained large language model (LLM) extraction, evidence checking, entity alignment, and graph export. Generated descriptions and local subgraph summaries are constrained by source evidence and encoded with the BGE-m3 text embedding model. A relation-aware graph attention encoder provides structural representations, which are projected into a shared space and combined with semantic representations through a relation-conditioned gate. Link prediction and relation classification provide the principal quantitative evaluations. The Chinese historical-cultural collection illustrates the protocol with 6,744 normalized entities and 46,284 retained triples from 10,998 text entries. The fusion model achieves a mean reciprocal rank of 0.624, Hits@10 of 0.828, and a relation-classification macro-F1 of 0.865. Baseline and ablation comparisons indicate complementary contributions from structural and semantic information. Application to another collection involves language-appropriate preprocessing, a domain-specific ontology, documented alignment decisions, and evaluation that controls shared-source information across data partitions.

unique.title: "Can AI Predict the 'Diversity Premium'? Reassessing Knowledge Diversity in NSF Grant Proposals Through Large Language Models
LLM Homogenisation
Introducing Cultural Knowledge in Language Models: KazCulture Dataset for Kazakh Culture
unique.abstract: Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved significant advances in linguistic fluency, they often suffer from a lack of cultural knowledge associated with low-resource languages. This deficiency could challenge their integration into high-stakes applications across diverse regions. In this paper, we present a systematic method for embedding nation-specific cultural knowledge into LLMs, using Kazakh culture and language as a case study. We present KazCulture, a robust Kazakh culture-specific dataset composed of 16,137 human-crafted Passage-Question-Answer (PQA) triplets. KazCulture is rigorously curated from 11 books related to culture and the Koshpendiler.kz digital archive, capturing deep cultural semantics in areas such as customs, traditions, beliefs, cuisine, and household practices. Using KazCulture, we evaluated 36 LLMs, including proprietary frontier models and open-source alternatives. Our benchmarking reveals a critical disparity: while proprietary models like GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5-Pro achieved up to 80% accuracy, open-source models struggled significantly. To bridge this gap, we propose a two-stage adaptation pipeline: 1) perform fine-tuning on a general multilingual dataset (ISSAI-SFT) for linguistic robustness, then 2) run targeted fine-tuning on KazCulture. This method boosted the accuracy of the Qwen3-32B model from a baseline of 39.51% to 64.54%. KazCulture provides a timely contribution to Artificial Intelligence (AI) research as both a rigorous benchmark for Kazakh-culture-related knowledge and a training resource to develop different culture aware LLMs. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/issai/KazCulture.

unique.title: Human-AI Interaction in L2 Writing Support: Homogenization in LLM Revisions of Learner Errors
unique.abstract: This study examines whether different large language models revise the same L2 learner errors in similar ways. The dataset included 100 error units from IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 responses written by Chinese EFL learners. Each error unit was revised by 3 mainstream Large language models (LLMs): GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, and Gemini Flash to test how similar their outputs are. Two measuring methods were introduced to do the analysis: BERTScore F1 was used to measure similarity in meaning, and Jaccard Similarity was used to measure overlap in wording. The study also examined whether learner-language features were retained, reformulated, or removed after revision. The results show clear similarity across the three models, especially at the meaning level. Grammar-related and collocation errors produced the most similar revisions. The findings suggest that LLM-based revision can improve accuracy and fluency, but it can also overlook interlanguage features for the purpose of standardized writing. LLM feedback is therefore better used for comparison and reflection than as a final answer.
unique.journal: Journal of Humanities Arts and Social Science

unique.title: B1 2026Q1 FULL25 — Analysis and Materials Registration: LLM Forecast-Error Homogenization
unique.abstract: This registration archives the materials for the B1 2026Q1 FULL25 measurement exercise on LLM forecast-error homogenization. It includes the frozen prediction file, checksum, SEC EDGAR/XBRL truth file, and Python analysis script. The full registration document is uploaded as OSF_预注册正文.md. This is an analysis and materials registration, not a prospective pre-registration.

unique.title: Epistemic injustice and phenomenological reductionism in psychiatric AI: an empirical-philosophical analysis
Impersonal Statements: LLM-Era College Admissions Essays Exhibit Deep Homogenization Despite Lexical Diversity
unique.abstract: Concerns that AI will homogenize human thinking—and homogenization findings in lab contexts—appear at odds with findings that AI-assisted content is judged as highly original. Using a multi-method approach that combined a controlled experiment with two large-scale natural experiments in over 160,000 U.S. college admissions essays, we observed a counterintuitive pattern: AI-assisted essays and essays written after the release of ChatGPT showed greater lexical diversity, but the increasingly diverse words actually expressed increasingly homogeneous ideas. This “paradoxical homogenization” pattern was robust across demographic subgroups but emerged disproportionately among applicants outside racial and linguistic mainstreams. Event-time analyses and robustness checks ruled out pre-existing trends and pandemic-related confounds. The findings suggest that surface-level diversity of AI-generated content masks deeper constraints on the breadth of human ideation. Extending lab-based AI homogenization research, paradoxical homogenization appears to have reached real-world, high-stakes contexts where writing is expressly personal and AI use is explicitly prohibited.

unique.title: The Cultural Person A Conceptual Framework for Understanding LLM-Based Artificial Intelligence as the Communicative Mediator of Humanity's Aggregated Cultural Knowledge
Generative AI tools in reflective essays: Moderating moral injuries and epistemic injustices
unique.abstract: The emergence of large language models such as ChatGPT is already influencing health care delivery, research and training for the next cohort of health care professionals. In a consumer-driven market, their capabilities to generate new forms of knowing and doing for experts and novices present both promises and threats to the livelihood of patients. This article explores burdens imposed by the use of generative artificial intelligence tools in reflective essays submitted by a fifth of first-year health sciences students. In a curriculum centred around Vision 2030 at a South African university, deviations from prescribed guidelines in an essay requiring students to demonstrate an understanding of the models of disability are presented as moral injuries and epistemic injustices. Considering our obligations as educators to contribute to a humanising praxis, the author evaluates an eroded trust between educators and students and offers an interim solution for attaining skills in academic literacy in a developing country.Contribution: This article provides health sciences educators with an opportunity to pause and reflect on how they would like to integrate generative AI tools into their assessments.

unique.title: The Standardization of the Digital Dialect: Artificial Intelligence, Epistemic Injustice, and the Future of Linguistic Diversity
unique.abstract: Language has historically functioned as both a communicative system and a repository of cultural identity, social memory, and collective belonging. In the contemporary digital era, Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies increasingly mediate communication practices through predictive text systems, speech recognition software, algorithmic moderation, and Large Language Models (LLMs). Although such technologies have improved efficiency, accessibility, and multilingual interaction, emerging scholarship suggests that AI systems may also reproduce existing linguistic hierarchies by privileging dominant and standardized language forms while marginalizing dialectal and non-standard varieties (Helm et al., 2024; Hofmann et al., 2024). This theoretical paper examines how AI-driven communication systems may contribute to processes of linguistic standardization and dialect marginalization within digital environments. Drawing upon Fricker’s (2007) theory of epistemic injustice, the paper introduces the concept of the Digital Language Divide to explain disparities in computational recognition, linguistic legitimacy, and technological visibility among speech communities. Unlike deterministic arguments that portray technology solely as a force of linguistic erosion, this paper adopts a balanced perspective acknowledging that AI technologies may simultaneously expand communication access while also reinforcing structural inequalities in language representation. Recent empirical studies demonstrate that some AI systems exhibit dialect prejudice, particularly toward speakers of African American English and other non-standard language varieties (Hofmann et al., 2024). Additionally, emerging scholarship on techno-linguistic bias argues that language technologies frequently prioritize dominant linguistic norms embedded within training datasets (Helm et al., 2024). Building upon these findings, this paper theorizes how algorithmic standardization may gradually influence linguistic practices, educational expectations, and communicative participation within digitally mediated societies. This paper seeks to establish a conceptual foundation for future interdisciplinary inquiry into the sociolinguistic consequences of AI-mediated communication. The study concludes by proposing directions for future empirical research, policy development, and inclusive AI design frameworks capable of supporting linguistic diversity within digital ecosystems.
unique.journal: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Applied Science

unique.title: Epistemic Injustice in Generative AI: Probabilistic Generation, Trust Erosion, and the Structural Conditions of Algorithmic Knowledge Harm
unique.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence, and large language models (LLMs) in particular, are increasingly deployed as epistemic intermediaries across domains ranging from legal research to clinical decision support. This paper argues that LLMs produce a distinctive form of epistemic injustice- understood, following Fricker, as a wrong done to agents specifically in their capacity as knowers-through three interrelated structural mechanisms: (1) automation-induced testimonial injustice (AITI), whereby the confident and fluent outputs of LLMs systematically deflate the credibility accorded to competing human testimony; (2) interpretive erasure, whereby the probabilistic compression of training corpora marginalises minority epistemic frameworks through a dynamic process that simultaneously reflects and actively widens existing hermeneutical gaps; and (3) epistemic debt accumulation, whereby sustained reliance on AI-mediated knowledge progressively erodes individual and collective epistemic competence. Drawing on Fricker's canonical framework, Dotson's account of epistemic violence, and Bender et al.'s critique of stochastic parrots, the paper further introduces the concept of Algorithmic Gettier Cases (AGCs)-instances in which LLM outputs are accidentally true yet epistemically defective-as an analytical device for exposing the structural failure modes of probabilistic generation. The paper concludes with a fourcomponent governance framework oriented towards testimonial transparency, hermeneutical pluralism, competence preservation, and structural accountability in high-stakes deployment contexts, with each principle linked explicitly to the mechanism it is designed to address.

unique.title: Epistemic Injustice in Algorithmic Systems: A Frickerian Analysis of AI-Driven Knowledge Production
unique.abstract: Artificial intelligence is playing a great role in the production, classification, retrieval, and communication of knowledge. Tools like large language models, recommender systems, automated decision-making systems, and search engines do more than just process information; they shape whose testimony is heard, which concepts become available for interpreting experience, and which claims are treated as credible or important. This paper argues that Miranda Fricker's theory of epistemic injustice offers a strong framework to ethically identify shortcomings in AI-enabled knowledge production; however, it also suggests that, the distinction made in classical accounts between testimonial and hermeneutical injustices needs to be extended in order to address them in the context of sociotechnical systems. Testimonial injustice can arise when algorithmic models reproduce credibility deficits through biased training data, proxy variables, ranking practices, moderation systems, or automated classification. On the other hand, hermeneutical injustice can emerge when certain communities are poorly represented in the conceptual and linguistic tools that AI systems use to create explanations, categories, and interpretations. The paper further argues that the opaque nature of many AI systems intensifies these harms because affected persons may be unable to understand, contest, or correct the epistemic processes that affect them. Building on Fricker, Floridi, Dotson, Medina, and contemporary work in AI ethics, the paper develops an epistemic justice framework centred on adequacy in represantation, credibility protection, interpretive inclusion, contestability, provenance, and institutional accountability. The proposed framework treats epistemic justice not merely as a desirable output property but as a design and governance requirement for AI systems that participate in consequential knowledge practices.

unique.title: Hallucination as epistemic pollution: epistemic injustice and credibility in futures-oriented science education
unique.abstract: Abstract In this critical conceptual review, I ask what generative artificial intelligence does to the distribution of epistemic authority in futures-oriented science education. I argue that the phenomenon usually described as hallucination is best understood not as isolated error but as epistemic pollution; that is, as a cumulative degradation of the cues by which learners judge reliability. I draw on four literature domains that have developed largely in isolation, namely technical and critical work on hallucination in natural language generation, philosophical work on epistemic injustice, futures studies scholarship on futures literacy, and science education research on future scaffolding and epistemological access. I first distinguish classes of unsupported output and specify six conditions under which such output counts as pollution rather than ordinary error, namely (1) persistence after correction, (2) circulation at scale, (3) contamination of downstream reasoning, (4) degradation of shared credibility cues, (5) opacity of provenance, and (6) the externalisation of verification costs. I then position the large language model not as an epistemic agent but as a component within a classroom credibility infrastructure, and I identify three mechanisms through which pollution may become injustice: (i) credibility displacement, (ii) hermeneutical narrowing, and (iii) unequal verification labour. Because these are conceptual hypotheses rather than demonstrated classroom effects, I state the conditions under which each would constitute an injustice rather than a harm borne equally, and what evidence would test each. I finally advance five pedagogical design principles, namely (a) provenance first inquiry, (b) collective verification, (c) epistemic role protection, (d) uncertainty discipline, and (e) plural futures safeguards. I offer these principles as regulative ideas alongside a research agenda for their empirical evaluation.

unique.title: Algorithmic Orthodoxy and Gendered Scripture: AI, Biblical Interpretation, and Epistemic Injustice in the Global South
unique.abstract: Abstract This paper offers a critical, interdisciplinary examination of artificial intelligence ( AI ) as a theological mediator, arguing that AI systems do not merely transmit religious knowledge but actively reproduce gendered epistemic hierarchies embedded in their training data. Grounded in an African Technocultural Feminist framework and informed by feminist hermeneutics and critical AI studies, the study employs a qualitative, discourse-analytical method based on simulated interviews with major large language models. These prompts focus on women’s roles in church leadership, religious life in the Global South, and interpretations of Proverbs 31 and Ephesians 5:22–24, serving as test cases for identifying recurring algorithmic biases. The findings reveal a pattern described as “soft-neutral patriarchy,” where AI systems present balanced perspectives while subtly privileging dominant, often complementarian interpretations. Women are consistently represented in relation to domesticity, moral responsibility, and relational spirituality, while leadership roles are framed as conditional or exceptional. In interpretations of Proverbs 31, women’s agency is acknowledged but confined within domesticated and productivity-centered ideals. Similarly, readings of Ephesians 5:22–24 tend to soften hierarchical submission rhetorically while maintaining its structural logic, a tendency identified as “algorithmic equilibrium bias.” The study also shows how AI systems essentialize the Global South as inherently traditional, reinforcing colonial epistemic hierarchies and obscuring the diversity of African women’s lived experiences. Beyond biblical texts, the paper demonstrates how AI reproduces longstanding patriarchal distortions in representations of figures such as Mary Magdalene and Lilith, privileging sexualized or demonized portrayals over feminist reinterpretations. These dynamics are conceptualized as forms of testimonial injustice, hermeneutical erasure, and epistemic fragmentation, resulting in “algorithmic orthodoxy.” The paper concludes by advocating a decolonial reconfiguration of AI grounded in epistemic justice, indigenous knowledge systems, and participatory feminist design, positioning AI as a potential tool for theological liberation and gender justice in the Global South.

unique.title: Generative AI Meets Open-Ended Survey Responses: Research Participant Use of AI and Homogenization
unique.abstract: The growing popularity of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools presents new challenges for data quality in online surveys and experiments. This study examines participants’ use of large language models to answer open-ended survey questions and describes empirical tendencies in human versus large language model (LLM)-generated text responses. In an original survey of research participants recruited from a popular online platform for sourcing social science research subjects, 34 percent reported using LLMs to help them answer open-ended survey questions. Simulations comparing human-written responses from three pre-ChatGPT studies with LLM-generated text reveal that LLM responses are more homogeneous and positive, particularly when they describe social groups in sensitive questions. These homogenization patterns may mask important underlying social variation in attitudes and beliefs among human subjects, raising concerns about data validity. Our findings shed light on the scope and potential consequences of participants’ LLM use in online research.

unique.title: Machine-Translating Feminism: Generative AI, Epistemic Injustice, and the Politics of Gendered Meaning in Indonesian Feminist Discourse
unique.abstract: In transnational feminist knowledge circuits, generative AI has become a decisive yet insufficiently theorised mediator of gendered meaning across languages. Large language models do not simply transfer words between Indonesian and English; they set the moral, political, and gendered conditions under which feminist vocabularies become intelligible. This article intervenes at the intersection of feminist translation studies, epistemic injustice theory, and multilingual AI critique to theorise what we term machine-translating feminism: the process through which generative AI translates feminist language while reformatting feminism into a more manageable discursive object. Departing from English-centric AI bias scholarship, we turn to Indonesian feminist discourse as a Global South site where womanhood, sexuality, violence, and anti-feminist backlash are mediated through contested vocabularies. Through close readings of Ayu Utami’s Saman and Leila S. Chudori’s Laut Bercerita, alongside public feminist vocabularies, the article identifies four diagnostic patterns of translational distortion: lexical neutralisation, moral simplification, depoliticisation of structural violence, and patriarchal overcoding. The analysis shows how generative AI operates as a translation regime rather than a neutral tool, producing what we term patriarchal legibility: a mode of readability in which feminist conflict becomes internationally consumable by becoming less threatening to patriarchal, institutional, and Anglophone interpretive regimes.

unique.title: Silenced in the Data: Epistemic Injustice as Challenge for the AI-Assisted Analysis of Abuse in the Catholic Church
unique.abstract: This is the presentation of the long paper "Silenced in the Data: Epistemic Injustice as Challenge for the AI-Assisted Analysis of Abuse in the Catholic Church" as presented at DH 2026 in Daejeon, South Korea on July 31st 2026. Abstract: This study examines epistemic injustice in Catholic Church abuse discourse, focusing on marginalized adult women survivors. Using AI-assisted methods, we create an annotated corpus, apply zero-shot relevance detection with generative LLMs, and perform fine-grained classification. Results reveal hidden patterns, data sparsity, and methodological strategies for analyzing small, imbalanced datasets. The project “Von Epistemic Injustice zu Epistemic Awareness. Prozessbasierte Methodenforschung zuMissbrauch an erwachsenen Frauen in der katholischen Kirche” (From Epistemic Injustice to EpistemicAwareness. Process‑based Methodological Research on Abuse of Adult Women in the Catholic Church) isfunded by the DFG (German Research Association, project number 539293243):https://missbrauchsmuster.de/forschen/projekte/forschungsprojekt-von-epistemic-injustice-zu-epistemic-awareness-prozessbasierte-methodenforschung-zu-missbrauch-an-erwachsenen-frauen-in-der-katholischen-kirche/ More information on the Missbrauchsmuster website.
unique.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

unique.title: Epistemic Injustice in Generative AI: How Minority Language Systems Reproduce or Resist Digital Exclusion
unique.abstract: Generative AI performance disparities can exclude minority-language speakers from digital participation. Drawing on Fricker’s epistemic-injustice framework, we examined five Chinese minority languages using four-way causal mediation decomposition, intersectional analysis, and participatory evaluation. Under the measured mediators and model specification, non-PIE components accounted for an average of 67.5% of observed disparities. Tibetan speech recognition yielded a 43.9% word error rate (WER) for elderly speakers using religious and dialectal language, 6.9 percentage points above the main-effects additive reference. Community evaluation prioritized religious sensitivity, while threshold rules identified culturally salient failures missed by linear weighting. CAML-LLM, integrating cultural knowledge graphs, multimodal alignment, and community-weighted training, reduced WER from 31.2% to 22.7% and improved cultural appropriateness by 22.5%. These findings characterize model-dependent disparities and demonstrate that participatory system design can improve minority-language performance within the evaluated settings.

unique.title: Writing homogenization post-ChatGPT: Corpus evidence from a decade-long study
unique.abstract: Description: This repository contains supplementary computational materials for the manuscript Generative AI and the Emergence of Hybrid Authorship in academic writing: A Corpus-Based Analysis (2015–2024) published in the Modern Language Journal. The files provide complete R scripts for machine learning classification and statistical evaluation. The code operationalizes multidimensional feature extraction across learner corpora. It establishes a robust and reproducible methodological framework. Researchers can adopt this computational architecture using independent historical archives. This application establishes a known baseline of unaided human authorship. Consequently, educators can objectively quantify the impact of algorithmic text generation. The provided algorithms isolate the specific linguistic footprint of hybrid authorship. This repository ensures full computational reproducibility for the broader academic community.

unique.title: Recursive Artificial Intelligence Training and the Homogenization of Discourse
unique.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) begin to produce text on the internet, the same repository from which training data for LLMs are scraped, LLMs will start to train on data they produced. What will happen to future models when LLMs are trained on their own text? Scholars have raised concerns about the possibility that LLMs homogenize language and discourse. These concerns are further exaggerated as LLMs begin to infect their own repositories, marking a turn from human-produced training data sets. In this paper I simulate a recursive training loop by prompting a popular open-source LLM with 1000 prompts and using the output to train the same LLM, creating Model-1. I repeat this process 5 times. I then analyze these outputs through the lens of Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA), a methodology which attempts to analyze discourse in terms of genre (social action), discourse (topic representation), and style (authorial identity). I argue that recursive training results in an increase in homogeneity, in which later outputs tend to resemble each other in terms of both vocabulary (measured through Type-Token Ratio and Self-BLEU) and format (later generations unilaterally adopt features like extensive footnotes and institutional affiliation).

unique.title: Beyond Spin: Automated Homogenisation and the Case for Engineered Friction
Whose Knowledge Becomes the Tourism Story: Generative AI, Local Knowledge, and the Future of Tourism
unique.abstract: This systematic review examines how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) may influence local knowledge in tourism, focusing on algorithmic mediation, epistemic authority, and representational justice. Synthesizing 35 articles across four literature streams published primarily between 2023 and 2026, covering AI technologies, local knowledge systems, computational mediation, and cultural representation, the paper examines how conversational travel agents and large language models may influence destination storytelling. The synthesis indicates that GenAI can function as an active intermediary rather than simply as a neutral information channel. Eleven operational transformations are identified, including selection, translation, de-contextualization, recombination, and redistribution, through which local knowledge may be altered as it moves into AI-mediated tourism environments. The review suggests that these processes may reproduce existing differences in tourism knowledge visibility, particularly where AI systems rely heavily on digitally available and commercially prominent information while local, oral, or less digitally represented knowledge remains comparatively less visible. The literature also identifies concerns regarding AI-generated inaccuracies, including historical hallucinations and cultural simplification, and suggests that the fluency of AI-generated content may contribute to perceptions of authority among users. From a knowledge governance perspective, the synthesis raises concerns about the implications of extracting and processing traditional and Indigenous knowledge without adequate community participation, consent, attribution, or benefit-sharing, particularly in relation to Indigenous Data Sovereignty. Rather than concluding that GenAI inevitably displaces traditional knowledge authorities, the review suggests that it may introduce an additional layer of influence through which tourists encounter and evaluate destination knowledge. To address these concerns, the paper proposes a six-pillar Responsible AI Governance Framework encompassing cultural sensitivity, transparency, inclusivity, community-informed co-design, platform accountability, and respect for local ownership. The review concludes that responsible integration of GenAI in tourism requires greater attention to human oversight, community participation, knowledge governance, and the rights of local knowledge holders.

unique.title: The Homogenizing Engine: AI's Role in Standardizing Culture and the Path to Policy
unique.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as unprecedented drivers of cultural homogenization, operating at scales and speeds that exceed all previous technologies. This paper examines how LLMs reduce cultural diversity across three cultural domains. Drawing on recent empirical studies, we demonstrate that LLMs disproportionately reflect a narrow demographic, primarily western, liberal, high-income, highly educated, male populations from English-speaking nations, while marginalizing not only non-Western cultures but also diverse groups within Western societies, including older adults, religious communities, and minority populations. Unlike earlier technologies that primarily transmitted cultural content, LLMs actively shape communication styles and knowledge systems, creating a feedback loop where AI-generated content becomes training material for future systems, progressively standardizing human expression with each generation. These homogenizing effects extend beyond representation to behavioral influence, reshaping how users communicate and make decisions. We propose targeted policy interventions across the LLM development pipeline and emphasize the critical need for standardized benchmarks to evaluate how well LLMs understand and represent diverse cultures across all stages. These interventions require coordinated action among AI developers, policymakers, social scientists, and diverse cultural communities to ensure that cultural diversity becomes a non-negotiable requirement rather than an optional enhancement. Without such efforts, AI risks eroding humanity's cultural plurality, replacing diverse traditions with homogenized norms shaped by a narrow subset of the global population.
unique.journal: Policy Insights from the Behavioral and Brain Sciences

unique.title: Generative AI Meets Open-Ended Survey Responses: Research Participant Use of AI and Homogenization
unique.abstract: The growing popularity of generative AI tools presents new challenges for data quality in online surveys and experiments. This study examines participants’ use of large language models to answer open-ended survey questions and describes empirical tendencies in human vs LLM-generated text responses. In an original survey of participants recruited from a popular online platform for sourcing social science research subjects, 34% reported using LLMs to help them answer open-ended survey questions. Simulations comparing human-written responses from three pre-ChatGPT studies with LLM-generated text reveal that LLM responses are more homogeneous and positive, particularly when they describe social groups in sensitive questions. These homogenization patterns may mask important underlying social variation in attitudes and beliefs among human subjects, raising concerns about data validity. Our findings shed light on the scope and potential consequences of participants’ LLM use in online research.

unique.title: CRIXP: Cultural Knowledge Representation for Inherent eXPlainability
unique.abstract: Cultural awareness plays a vital role in making AI systems beneficial for a globalized audience. This cultural awareness is lacking in modern decision-support systems and in the current state of the work, where explainability is the paramount requirement now from all AI systems. To address this, the article introduces CRIXP, a framework with decisive cultural knowledge and the capability to explain the reasoning behind its suggestions. CRIXP comprises: 1) a cultural ontology (CRO); 2) a cultural knowledge graph (CKG); 3) a general-purpose adaptable algorithm providing recommendations and explanations; and 4) a CKG enrichment module. The cultural traits of all the locales are consolidated and represented as an ontology and a knowledge graph. A cultural shift suggestion system has been demonstrated for recommendations and explanations. The response generated is compared with ChatGPT. CRIXP is found to outperform ChatGPT by providing more relevant recommendations with inherent explainability.
unique.journal: IEEE Transactions on Computational Social Systems

unique.title: Lost in Translation, Lost in Nation: AI-Induced Linguistic Homogenisation as a Threat to Rastravadah
unique.abstract: In Indian philosophy, Rastravadah is not a single, unified identity but a collection of many identities. This idea depends on the coexistence of India’s many languages, dialects, and ways of speaking. This paper examines a subtle threat to that foundation: how AI can make language more uniform. Large language models are mostly trained on widely used languages and tend to prefer the most standard forms. As a result, they often smooth out regional expressions, dialects, and cultural details in translation, writing, and daily communication. More people are using these tools to write or translate in Tamil, Malayalam, Hindi, and other Indian languages. Over time, their language starts to sound more average and less unique. This slow change weakens the special qualities that have shaped India’s diverse national identity. This article argues that this threat to Rastravadah comes from the tools we use every day, not from official policies. First, it explains how Indian nationhood is built on linguistic diversity. Next, it examines how AI can make language more uniform, focusing on training data and patterns in AI output. Finally, it discusses what this means for teaching and language policy, and suggests solutions like developing regional language models and teaching critical AI skills in language classes. The paper brings together ideas from philosophy, nationhood, and AI to discuss India’s linguistic and cultural diversity.

unique.title: Language ideologies and the homogenizing pull of generative AI
The Artificial Hivemind: Rethinking Work Design and Leadership in the Age of Homogenized AI
unique.abstract: This article examines the organizational implications of behavioral homogeneity in large language models (LLMs), a phenomenon we term the "Artificial Hivemind." Drawing on a comprehensive analysis of 26,000 real-world user queries and 70+ language models, we reveal that contemporary AI systems exhibit pronounced intra-model repetition and inter-model convergence, generating strikingly similar outputs despite variations in architecture, training, and scale. From an organizational leadership and work design perspective, this convergence poses critical challenges: the erosion of creative diversity in AI-assisted workflows, the potential amplification of groupthink in decision-making processes, and misalignment between organizational needs for pluralistic solutions and AI capabilities. We introduce evidence-based organizational responses spanning leadership communication strategies, work redesign initiatives, and governance frameworks. Our findings demonstrate that current reward models and AI evaluation systems are miscalibrated to human preferences when responses exhibit comparable quality but divergent styles—a critical gap for organizations deploying AI at scale. This research provides practitioners with actionable frameworks for diagnosing AI homogenization in their workflows, redesigning roles to preserve human creativity, and building governance structures that promote cognitive diversity rather than algorithmic conformity.

unique.title: Generative AI and Content Homogenization: The Case of Digital Marketing
The Algorithmic accent: investigating the homogenization of linguistic identity in AI-mediated classrooms
unique.abstract: AI has become ubiquitous in schools, and personalised learning carries a cost that is rarely discussed: the flattening of student identity. This paper examines the algorithmic accent - the way Large Language Models (LLMs) often default to a standardized, Western-centric linguistic style that can overshadow diverse student voices. The technology is quick. But that speed comes with a quieter effect: it eliminates local dialects and cultural speaking style along the way. Most research so far asks only whether students achieve improved grades using AI; how this impacts a student's sense of self, and their ability to negotiate multiple cultures, remains an enormous gap. We report on a two-month, teacher-led observation of 15 university students (semesters 1-5) enrolled in an academic writing course at an academy in Pakistan, all of whom gave informed consent to participate. Drawing on translanguaging (Wei, 2018) and the concept of Global English standardisation (Agarwal et al., 2025), we suggest these tools function as a filter rather than a mirror. Students are led to exchange their own voice for the words of the algorithm-more fluent, perhaps, but missing the social texture that makes a language human. We recommend a pedagogical approach in which AI becomes a tool for exploring language, not a template for conforming to it. / Keywords: algorithmic accent, linguistic identity, linguistic homogenization, translanguaging, ai-mediated classrooms

unique.title: Countering AI homogenisation: Developing adaptable writers through multi-genre pedagogy
unique.abstract: As AI-assisted writing tools become an increasingly routine presence in higher education, concerns have emerged about the homogenisation of academic writing in terms of style, genre, and discipline. By outsourcing creativity and voice to LLMs—which have no access to the nuances of students’ writing contexts—we risk stifling our students and limiting their potential to develop into agile, adaptable writers, capable of deftly managing linguistic choices for specific research communities and genres. In this context, we propose a novel approach to teaching academic writing, known as multi-genre pedagogy (MGP). In MGP, we apply the principles for effective task design outlined by Swales and Feak (2023) to develop tasks that require students to recontextualise their writing for different audiences and purposes through varied genres. Rather than remaining tethered to prototypical fixed-genre models—which can be readily conjured up by LLMs—this pedagogy requires a human-centred approach, sensitive to the situated nature of writing and the specific institutional, disciplinary, and communicative contexts in which students operate. If AI risks promoting an homogenisation of writing, this approach is calibrated towards cultivating the opposite: stretching students to diversify their writing in response to the unfamiliar and evolving communicative demands of contemporary academia.Our project draws on the framework developed by Tardy et al. (2020), which conceptualizes genre knowledge and metacognition as key components of effective recontextualisation. We distinguish between genre-specific knowledge and genre awareness, an adaptable understanding of how genres function. These forms of knowledge interact with metacognitive processes, particularly writers’ ability to monitor and regulate their own strategies when navigating unfamiliar communicative demands. By foregrounding recontextualisation rather than static mastery, this framework supports a pedagogical shift from writing within genres to writing across them, an approach well-suited to the disciplinary and communicative challenges of the present moment.Our project draws from data collected from doctoral students in Sweden, the United Kingdom, the United States, and Norway. Drawing on student writing, classroom recordings, and interviews, we aim to assess both the pedagogical impact of MGP and the metacognitive processes it may activate. By comparing cases across national and institutional contexts, we seek to identify how MGP supports students in developing transferable writing strategies.We will share task examples and emerging insights from the initial stages of the project and reflect on the methodological challenges and opportunities of evaluating writing transfer in authentic classroom settings where AI-assisted tools increasingly form part of students’ writing environments. Rather than treating AI use as a variable to be controlled or an affordance to be exploited, the study de-centres LLMS and focuses on the role of teachers and their professional judgment in designing and sustaining pedagogical practices that foreground rhetorical choice and context-sensitive adaption. Ultimately, the project aims to inform L2 writing and EAP course design by demonstrating how multi-genre pedagogy can support the development of adaptable, rhetorically aware writers while maintaining writing as a meaningful human practice in evolving academic contexts.

unique.title: Unveiling the inverted-U shape: how firm knowledge diversity influences the industry distance of CVC investment
unique.abstract: Purpose In the era of a knowledge-driven economy, corporate venture capital (CVC) has emerged as a vital mechanism for fostering innovation and strategic growth among incumbents. However, a crucial aspect that has been somewhat overlooked is why incumbents choose to invest in technology ventures in specific areas rather than others. This study aims to fill this gap by exploring the relationship between firm knowledge diversity and the strategy of CVC investment based on the knowledge-based view. Design/methodology/approach The authors’ analysis is based on data covering CVC investments from established Chinese manufacturing firms. The authors integrated data from CV Source, IncoPat, the Chinese Research Data Services Platform and China Stock Market and Accounting Research (CSMAR) to create the data set. Given the discrepancy between the industry classifications for startups in CV Source and those for investors in CSMAR, we implemented a large language model to analyze textual business descriptions of startups to map them onto industry codes consistent with the National Economic Industry Classification system used by CSMAR. Findings The empirical results reveal that incumbents’ knowledge diversity has an inverted U-shaped effect on the industry distance of CVC investments. Moreover, technological dynamism and CEO tenure negatively moderate this curvilinear relationship. These findings contribute to strategic management theory and have implications for corporate investment strategies. Originality/value This study advances the CVC literature by revealing a nonlinear relationship between firm knowledge diversity and industry distance of CVC investments, while taking into account boundary conditions.

unique.title: NED-GraphRAG for Evidence-Constrained Traditional Dress Design: Integrating User Needs with Cultural Knowledge Graphs
unique.abstract: Abstract Traditional dress design based on historical culture requires evidence that can be used within a specific design context and traced back to its source. Focusing on literati gatherings in the Song dynasty, this study develops NED-GraphRAG, a GraphRAG framework that incorporates contemporary user needs into the retrieval and use of cultural evidence. User needs were identified from 3,052 public online comments using BERTopic, coding assisted by a large language model, and researcher review. The Analytic Hierarchy Process was then conducted with 18 target users to determine the relative importance of cultural elements under three design need orientations: Historical Verification, Visual Communication, and Social Ritual. Evidence drawn from historical texts, images, cultural relic materials, and modern scholarship was standardized into 2,053 evidence units and organized into a cultural evidence graph containing 4,233 nodes, 12,749 relationships, and 854 manually verified semantic triples. Six retrieval methods were evaluated using 30 test queries. NED-GraphRAG achieved an nDCG@10 of 0.821 and an AHP-AS@5 of 0.852, exceeding GraphRAG Retrieval by 0.031 and 0.104, respectively. Claim support precision reached 0.897, and the user task success rate was 92.2%. The results show that user needs can be reflected in evidence priority while the underlying cultural evidence remains unchanged. Graph relations and source controls further support the traceability of evidence used in design recommendations. The framework provides a practical method for using cultural evidence in the contemporary design of traditional dress.

unique.title: Generative artificial intelligence drives large model generation algorithm for enhancing Chinese modern traditional cultural knowledge
unique.abstract: Abstract To address outdated knowledge, cultural-context mismatch, weak evidence linkage, and unsupported expansion in general-purpose large language model generation of traditional-cultural content, this study proposes a generative AI-driven knowledge-enhanced generation algorithm. The method decouples a frozen Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct generator from an external dynamic knowledge base and uses a four-field semantic tag scheme covering cultural category, historical stage, regional origin, and application scenario. Candidate evidence is ranked by vector similarity, graph relations, tag consistency, source credibility, and conflict penalties, then assembled into a constrained prompt without modifying the internal attention layers of the frozen model. An incremental update mechanism combines source verification, conflict detection, and expert review, while factual consistency, cultural-context adaptability, and evidence coverage are used for post-generation verification. Experiments cover classical texts, cultural heritage objects, intangible cultural heritage crafts, traditional Chinese opera, and folk culture, with 1,080 factual question-answering samples and 360 contextual generation tasks. The proposed system achieves 88.61% factual accuracy, 95.28% answer relevance, 94.17% evidence faithfulness, and 92.50% cultural-context adaptability. After knowledge updating, accuracy on update-dependent questions rises from 58.67% to 91.33%. These results indicate that the proposed framework provides a traceable, context-sensitive generation pipeline while retaining a frozen generation model; between-system differences are interpreted descriptively because complete paired baseline predictions were not retained.

unique.title: Artificial Intelligence in Reclaiming and Preserving Hausa Language and Cultural Knowledge: An Academic Overview
unique.abstract: This study discussed an intersection of artificial intelligence (AI) and indigenous knowledge with reference to the Hausa language, especially how AI is mediating, influencing, and potentially disrupting culturally ingrained epistemologies in the academic context. While on one hand, AI is efficient in translation, text generation, and data processing, its effectiveness, on the other hand, depends on the availability of highly-resourced language datasets, which marginalise low-resource languages, distorting meaning and flattening epistemic and interpretative depth. Using a qualitative research methodology, this conceptual analysis examines AI-produced Hausa texts and draws on previous studies to identify problems in linguistic representation. Observations from 15 respondents (researchers and students) reveal a series of problems in the context of linguistic representation, tonal accuracy, and culturally-based interpretation. Informed by cultural hermeneutics, it becomes clear that AI is unable to reproduce the contextual, moral, and philosophical richness in Hausa proverbs and written poetry, oral narratives, and the ‘Ajami’ manuscripts. Using the ChatGPT tool to translate some Hausa words and proverbs, the results reveal that indigenous knowledge has been reiterated into Hausa-based AI corpora, with online archiving and humanities-driven partnerships between linguists and AI engineers.
